opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for me the Circuits thread was really the moment where interpretability went from being kind of a vague aspiration to feeling like an actual science. Before that, a lot of the work was things like saliency maps or attribution methods, where you'd get a heatmap over an image and it would tell you, roughly, "the model was looking here." That's useful, but it doesn't tell you *how* the model is computing anything. It's a bit like knowing which part of the brain lights up without knowing what the neurons are actually doing.

What Chris Olah and the team did with the Circuits work on InceptionV1 was take the stance that neural networks aren't inscrutable blobs. They're made of parts, and those parts can be understood. They went in and found individual neurons that detected curves, and then they showed how those curve detectors were built up from earlier edge detectors, with actual weights you could read off and reason about. Then they found things like high-low frequency detectors, dog head detectors, car detectors assembled from wheels and windows. You could trace the algorithm the network had learned, almost like reverse-engineering a compiled program.

I think that framing matters enormously. It made three claims that became the foundation for the field: that features are the fundamental unit of a network, that features are connected into circuits through weights, and that there's universality, meaning similar features and circuits show up across different models. If those claims hold even approximately, then understanding a model becomes a tractable engineering problem rather than something hopeless.

It also surfaced the hard problems early. They ran into polysemantic neurons, single neurons responding to several unrelated things, which pointed toward superposition. A lot of the later work, sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning, the move from neurons to features as the unit of analysis, really traces back to grappling with what that thread uncovered.

So when people ask where to start, I point them there, not because everything in it was right, but because it set the ambition and the methodology. It said: we can actually look inside and understand what these systems are doing, mechanistically, and here's what that looks like in practice. And for anyone who cares about making these models reliable and safe, that's exactly the kind of understanding we need.

r002.rationale: It says features connect into circuits through weights, but does not explain circuits as features firing together to form higher-order concepts.

r003.rationale: It explicitly defines universality as similar features and circuits appearing across different models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's because Circuits was the first time someone made the claim concrete. Before that, interpretability was mostly saliency maps and feature visualizations, and you could always argue about whether you were looking at something real or just a pretty picture. What Chris Olah and that group did was say: look, there are individual neurons in InceptionV1 that detect curves, and you can trace how they're built out of earlier edge detectors, and you can trace how they feed into later shape detectors. And then they went and actually checked. They'd look at the weights, they'd hand-write the curve detector, they'd run ablations, and the predictions held up.

So the big idea was that a neural network isn't a black box you have to study from the outside. It's more like a program that someone compiled without leaving the source code, and the Circuits thread was a bet that you could decompile it. Features are the variables, circuits are the subroutines, and if you're patient enough you can read them off the weights.

The other reason I keep pointing people back to it is the epistemics. They were very upfront about the parts that didn't work cleanly. Polysemantic neurons were right there in the early papers, this annoying fact that one neuron would fire for cat faces and also the fronts of cars. They didn't hide it, they flagged it as the thing that was going to break the whole approach if nobody solved it. And that turned out to be exactly right. Superposition, dictionary learning, sparse autoencoders, all of that is downstream of taking that one loose end seriously.

And then there's just the culture it created. Those were Distill articles, interactive, with the actual weights you could poke at. It set this expectation that if you claim to understand a piece of a network, you should be able to show your work in a way other people can verify. I think that's why the field has stayed relatively honest compared to some other corners of ML. The starting point mattered.

r002.rationale: It describes detectors feeding into other detectors, but does not explain circuits as features firing together to form higher-order concepts.

r003.rationale: It does not mention similar circuits emerging across different neural networks.

astra-6.text:
I think the Circuits thread made the ambition of mechanistic interpretability concrete. Instead of just asking, “What inputs make this neuron activate?” it asked, “How do these neurons work together to produce a particular behavior?” That shifts the focus from describing a network to trying to reverse-engineer its computation.

And it showed what that could look like in practice: identify features, trace the connections between them, and build an explanation of how simpler features combine into more complex ones. You could start to see a neural network as something with internal structure that we might actually understand.

That doesn’t mean those early examples solved interpretability, or that the same methods automatically scale to much larger models. But they provided a concrete starting point—a set of examples and a way of asking questions that other researchers could build on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Circuits thread made the idea of understanding a neural network feel concrete. Instead of just asking what a model does, it asked: What are the actual mechanisms inside it that produce that behavior? Can we identify meaningful features, understand how they connect, and build up an explanation of a computation?

The vision examples were especially powerful because you could see those pieces—things like edge detectors combining into more complex features. That gave people both a conceptual framework and examples they could work through. It didn’t mean we suddenly understood entire networks, but it showed what a mechanistic explanation might look like and gave the field a starting point for pursuing one.
